office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The district: Cloverdale Community School Corporation serves Cloverdale Township in Putnam County and Jackson, Jennings and Taylor townships in Owen County [24]. Its main offices are at 310 E. Logan St. in Cloverdale [25]. Since 2020 it has also run the Cloverdale Distance Learning Academy (CDLA), a virtual school run with a private partner. Former Superintendent Greg Linton said CDLA grew from 174 students in 2020 to a little over 2,100 [26]. At the August 2026 budget workshop, Linton reported 1,013 in-person students in 2025-26, up 53 from the year before, and 2,053 CDLA students as of February 2026 [27]. State enrollment data, which include the virtual students, show 3,206 students in 2026, compared with 1,406 in 2022 [28].

Superintendent: Dr. Stacy Mason took over on July 1, 2026, on a three-year contract with a base salary of $123,500 [29]. She spent nearly 30 years with the Vigo County School Corporation [29]. She succeeded Greg Linton, superintendent for 12 years, who now leads CDLA [30]. In July 2026 the board approved an independent contractor agreement making Apex Education Services the chief financial officer and executive director of CDLA, with Linton serving in both roles [31].

Board: seven members. They are Vivian Whitaker (president), Mike Rightmyer II (vice president), Donna Fidler (secretary), Joe Mann, Katrina Lewis, Emily Haltom and Melissa Carrell [25]. Seats are tied to townships, but the whole district votes on every seat [24]. Cloverdale Township has four seats [24]. Three were filled in 2024, when Fidler, Lewis and Mann were re-elected over Aragon Gould [32, 33]. The Banner Graphic called those three seats at-large [34]. The fourth is Whitaker's seat, last elected in 2022 [35].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: ONE seat, the Cloverdale Township seat held by Whitaker. The state list says '1 seat', which matches the one-seat Cloverdale Township race in 2022 [6, 35]. Whitaker is running for re-election against Aragon Gould, a rematch of 2022, when Whitaker won 939 to 600 [36, 35]. The Banner Graphic reported that no candidate filed for the Taylor Township (Owen County) seat [36]. In an earlier race the paper noted that incumbents keep their seats in unfilled positions unless they resign [34].

Party labels: Gould is listed as Republican and Whitaker as Nonpartisan [6, 36]. In March 2025, the full board, including Whitaker, signed a letter opposing SB 287, the bill that allowed party labels in school board races. The letter said that 'to have members declare their political party would undermine the integrity of our decisions' [37].

Facilities and debt: in August 2026 the board approved a $4.5 million project to put synthetic turf on the football field and replace the track. Mason said the project would fix drainage problems and save on upkeep [27]. Mason estimated the net tax increase at about $0.0453 per $100 of assessed value. She said the district pays $1.36 million a year in debt service, falling to $1.17 million in 2036 [27]. On September 8, 2026 the board made a preliminary determination to issue up to $4,895,000 in bonds for district-wide renovations, including site and athletic improvements, equipment and technology [38]. A hearing on an amendment to the Cloverdale High School lease is set for October 12, 2026 [39].

Budget and taxes: at the August 2026 budget workshop, Linton reported an education fund balance of $5,823,521 at the start of 2026 and a proposed 2027 operations fund levy of $3,991,449 [27]. He said the district always advertises a higher tax rate than is finally approved. 'The rate this year is much lower than last year and that's due to us having solid cash balances,' he said [27]. The board held a budget hearing on August 24, 2026 and planned to adopt the budget on September 14 [40, 27]. This guide found no board statement on how the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) affects Cloverdale. The district is not listed among those with referendums on the November 2026 ballot [41].

Other 2026 decisions: in June 2026 the board added a special education teacher position at Cloverdale High School [30]. In August it adopted the SuperEval tool for superintendent evaluations [27]. A pre-bargaining hearing with the Cloverdale Education Association was held on September 9, 2026 [42].

Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum or questionnaire for this race. The most recent statements from both candidates are their 2022 Banner Graphic biographies and Whitaker's 2026 comments as board president [43].

candidates.summary: Challenger listed as Republican. Ran for this seat in 2022 and for a Cloverdale Township seat in 2024 [6, 35, 33].
background: Graduated from Cloverdale High School in 1994, according to his 2022 candidate biography [43].

Worked as an executive manager for a restaurant chain and as a regional manager for U.S. Bank, then served in the U.S. Army, including in Iraq in 2007-2008, and later in the Army Reserves as a squad leader, according to the 2022 biography [43].
In 2022 he worked as National Executive for Commercial Merchant Services with PNC Bank [43].
In 2022 he had a child at Cloverdale Elementary, coached youth football, basketball and baseball, and was treasurer of the Cloverdale Community Youth League [43].
path_to_ballot: Filed for the Cloverdale Township seat by the June 18, 2026 deadline, listed as Republican [36, 6].

Lost to Whitaker for this seat in 2022, 939 to 600 [35]. In 2024 he finished fourth of four candidates for three seats, with 1,352 votes. The Banner Graphic called these the board's at-large seats and the state's results list them under Cloverdale Township [32, 34, 33].

items: In 2022 he said he wanted to be 'a good steward of the resources that the town provides the school' [43].

In 2022 he said he wanted to help create 'a place where our children can learn the foundational skills need to launch a successful life' and to give students the skills to 'thrive in today's world' [43].

on_incumbent: This guide found no public statement from him on the current board's decisions.
plans: In 2022 he cited his experience in 'time management, managerial collaboration, financial stewardship, executive leadership' as preparation for the board [43].
gaps: No 2026 campaign website, questionnaire, forum answers or interview found. His stated positions come from his 2022 biography.
His current job was not confirmed for 2026.
The Republican label is as shown on the state list and the Banner Graphic list. This guide did not find whether a county party took any action on his candidacy.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and board president, on the board since the 2014 election, listed as Nonpartisan [25, 24, 6].
background: Retired educator. She graduated from Cloverdale High School in 1968 and earned three degrees from Indiana State University, according to her 2022 candidate biography [43].

Her career included teaching middle school physical science and high school chemistry, coaching girls' basketball and volleyball, and work as an athletic director, middle school assistant principal and principal, and assistant to the superintendent [43].
Board member since the 2014 election and board president [24, 25]. In 2026 she completed the Indiana School Boards Association's Board Presidents' Gold Seal Leadership Certification [44].
path_to_ballot: Filed for re-election to the Cloverdale Township seat by the June 18, 2026 deadline, listed as Nonpartisan [36, 6].
Won the seat in 2022 over Gould, 939 to 600 [35]. She ran unopposed in 2018 [45].

items: In 2022 she wrote that the board and superintendent 'must work together to stretch the available funds without raising taxes if possible,' and that 'the current board has done just that' [43].
In 2022 she said she intended 'to work with legislators to ensure that public schools receive funds proportionate to enrollment' [43].

In 2026 she said she is 'firmly against private schools or academies.' She said the board approved the CDLA virtual academy because its curriculum meets state standards, its students take state tests and each student is supervised by a licensed Indiana teacher. 'Now the money was attractive, but if we hadn't had those three things I wouldn't have been interested in it at all,' she said [26].

As president she signed the board's March 2025 letter opposing party labels in school board elections. The letter said members should be known 'by our reputation as strong supporters of our school community' [37].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member and the board president [25].
In 2026 she praised outgoing Superintendent Greg Linton: 'He knows his finances beyond anybody probably in the state of Indiana' [26].
On hiring Mason, she said she 'was looking for someone who had strengths outside of finance' [29].
She said the ISBA training introduced SuperEval, 'the tool we're using for our superintendent evaluations' [44].
plans: After winning in 2022 she pointed to raises, new course offerings, the Leader in Me program and preschool, and said she looked forward to 'building positive relations with the board and all of the faculty' [24].
In 2026 she said, 'I want to truly do what's best for kids' [44].
gaps: No 2026 campaign website, questionnaire or forum answers found.
Her 2026 comments were made as board president in news coverage, not as campaign statements.
